page10_img_1.png.title: Mind map of what 'Being technical' means for engineering managers
page10_img_1.png.description: A central box labelled “Being technical” is split into two main ideas: Comprehending (left) and Facilitation of (right). The Comprehending branch lists what managers need to understand — systems, tasks, tools, technologies, solutions, problems, and complexity. The Facilitation branch breaks into Growth (driving quality via mentoring and code review), Discussion (explaining rationale, providing or finding help, estimating effort), and Arbitrating (discussing design dilemmas by raising concerns, spotting flaws, and making suggestions). In the paper’s context this diagram illustrates that a manager’s technical knowledge is meant to enable informed conversations, mentoring, and arbitration rather than to replace engineers’ technical decision‑making.

page6_img_1.png.title: Conceptual framework of attributes for great engineering managers
page6_img_1.png.description: A two‑dimensional diagram that organizes the 15 identified manager attributes by manager function (rows: Cultivates, Motivates, Mediates) and by level of interaction (columns: with Individual; with Team/Organization). Under ‘Cultivates’ it lists: enables autonomy, supports experimentation, grows talent; under ‘Motivates’ it lists (individual) promotes fairness, builds relationship with team members, recognizes individuality and (team) maintains positive working environment, inspires the team; under ‘Mediates’ it lists (individual) clears path to execution and (team) facilitates external communication, drives alignment. Two attributes — “Is technical” and “Is available” — are shown as large enclosing bands around the matrix to indicate they support or are prerequisites for all other attributes. Icons (plant, smiley, bidirectional arrows) visually mark the three functions and the header “levels of interaction” labels the two interaction columns; the figure summarizes the paper’s conceptual grouping of what makes great software engineering managers.

page16_img_table_1.png.title: Mapping Google manager behaviours to this study's manager attributes
page16_img_table_1.png.description: A three-column table that aligns the manager behaviours identified in Google’s study (left) with their Google study descriptions (center) and the most closely matching manager attributes from this paper (right). Examples shown include: “Is a good coach” → Grows talent & Recognizes individuality; “Empowers team and does not micro-manage” → Enables autonomy; “Is productive and results-oriented” → Clears path to execution; and “Has important technical skills…” → Is technical. The table demonstrates substantial overlap between Google’s eight effective-manager behaviours and the 15 attributes derived here, with some Google behaviours mapping to multiple attributes and one (good communicator) noted as only a partial fit to this study’s “builds team culture,” highlighting both agreement and some domain-specific nuance.

page12_img_1.png.title: Demographic differences in importance ratings of manager attributes
page12_img_1.png.description: Table 3 reports statistically significant changes (coefficients) in how various demographics rate the importance of manager attributes, relative to baseline groups (male, U.S., engineers, etc.). Notable differences: Managers (vs. engineers) rate “builds a relationship with team members” (+1.21), “inspires the team” (+0.98), and “builds team culture” (+0.97) much higher; females (vs. males) place higher importance on “is technical” (+0.83) and “inspires the team” (+0.80). Regional differences include China (vs. U.S.) valuing “is technical” (+1.02) and “recognizes individuality” (+0.70), India valuing “builds team culture” (+0.99) and “builds a relationship” (+0.85) but less “grows talent” (−0.55), and Europe rating “drives alignment” (−0.53) and “recognizes individuality” (−0.50) lower. Two continuous effects show small negative changes per unit: each additional direct report associates with −0.01 for both “clears path to execution” and “enables autonomy,” and each additional year at Microsoft associates with −0.03 for “grows talent.”

page7_img_table_1.png.title: 15 Attributes of Great Engineering Managers
page7_img_table_1.png.description: A two-column table listing the 15 manager attributes the authors derived from interviews: each row names an attribute, gives a concise description of what it looks like in practice, and shows a short representative quote labeled by source (E = engineer, M = manager). Attributes shown include Is available; Is technical; Enables autonomy; Supports experimentation; Grows talent; Promotes fairness; Builds a relationship with team members; Recognizes individuality; Clears path to execution; Builds team culture; Guides the team; Maintains a positive working environment; Inspires the team; Facilitates external communication; and Drives alignment. Small icons in the table indicate whether an attribute relates to individual or team interaction and to the manager’s functions (cultivating engineering wisdom, motivating engineers, mediating communication). The paper uses this table as the operational definitions for a later survey — for example, those survey results found “maintains a positive working environment,” “grows talent,” and “enables autonomy” as the highest-rated attributes while “is technical” ranked near the bottom, underscoring the study’s conclusion that people-management attributes are most critical.

page11_img_1.png.title: Violin plots of importance ratings for 15 manager attributes (engineers vs managers)
page11_img_1.png.description: A series of violin plots (one per attribute, ordered by descending mean) showing how software engineers (top half of each violin) and engineering managers (bottom half) rated the importance of 15 attributes on a 1–10 scale; each plot includes a thick horizontal bar for the interquartile range and a short vertical tick for the mean. The highest-rated attributes are "maintains a positive working environment" (mean 9.05), "grows talent" (8.98), and "enables autonomy" (8.91), while "is technical" is near the bottom (7.84) and the lowest mean reported is for "builds relationships" (≈7.47). Most attributes show tight agreement (eleven attributes have an interquartile range of about two scale points), indicating consensus about their importance. The chart also reflects small but systematic differences between roles: engineering managers tend to give higher importance to motivational/team attributes (e.g., building relationships, inspiring the team, building culture — managers rate these higher by roughly +1.21, +0.98, and +0.97 respectively), which appears as slightly larger/shifted distributions in the managers’ halves of those violins.

page14_img_table_1.png.title: Table of attribute importance by discipline (relative to Software Engineering)
page14_img_table_1.png.description: This table presents the Software Engineering baseline mean importance scores (left column; N=563) for nine manager attributes (e.g., grows talent 8.93; inspires the team 8.43; drives alignment 8.33; builds team culture 8.13; is technical 7.89) and shows regression-based differences for five other knowledge-work disciplines (Business Programs & Operations, Finance, Marketing, Program Management, Sales). Positive values in the discipline columns indicate that that discipline rates an attribute higher than Software Engineering does; negative values indicate a lower rating. The table shows a consistent pattern: other disciplines place notably higher importance on “builds team culture”, “drives alignment” and “inspires the team” (deltas generally +0.36 to +0.88 across disciplines), while Software Engineering rates “clears path to execution” higher than Program Management (Program Management −0.38) and rates “is technical / is domain expert” higher than all other disciplines (other domains range ≈ −0.63 to −1.43). Sample sizes for each discipline are listed in the header (e.g., Business Programs & Operations N=193; Finance N=106; Marketing N=184; Program Management N=265; Sales N=266).

page4_img_1.png.title: Interview participants by role and experience (Table 1)
page4_img_1.png.description: The table enumerates the 37 interviewees (P1–P37) grouped by role (Engineer, Team Lead, Manager, Upper Manager) and by experience category (New vs Experienced). Cell contents list participant IDs: Engineers — New: P1–P5 (5); Experienced: P6, P7, P9, P18, P20, P23, P26 (7). Team Leads — New: P27, P30 (2); Experienced: P28, P31, P32 (3). Managers — New: P11, P12, P14, P17, P19, P21, P22, P25 (8); Experienced: P8, P10, P13, P15, P16, P24 (6). Upper Managers appear only in the Experienced column: P29, P33, P34, P35, P36, P37 (6). The parenthetical notes like “(out of 50)” indicate how many people were invited from each stratum (the recruitment pool), showing the authors used stratified purposeful sampling to obtain a diverse set of 37 interviewees across roles and experience levels.
